issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: Survival guilt implies an assault context involving other victims who died or a mass-casualty scenario, which is not supported anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the items describe interpersonal violation, hypervigilance, touch reactivity, and shame/control responses, making this appraisal hard to reconcile with the same assault presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: Being in nature as a salient trigger suggests the assault occurred in a natural/outdoor setting, but the rest of the profile instead centers on interpersonal closeness, touch, home-security checking, and scanning for danger. That outdoor-context trigger is insufficiently supported by the other selected items and feels disconnected from the overall assault formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window checking implies a home-intrusion or ongoing entry threat theme. That specific threat context is not reflected in the triggers or appraisals, which focus more on interpersonal intimacy and violation. As selected, it pulls toward a different assault scenario than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons points to a trauma meaningfully linked to armed perpetrators or authority/military cues. No other item supports that specific cue network; the profile otherwise emphasizes affection, emotional closeness, touch, guilt, helplessness, and control. This strategy appears to address a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

vignette:
Leilani Fono is a 66-year-old widowed Samoan-American woman who works as a network engineer for a regional telecommunications firm in suburban Oregon. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure she made to her primary care physician during a routine appointment, at which point her PCL-5 score of 75 indicated severe posttraumatic stress. She had not spoken about what happened to her in nearly two years.

Approximately twenty-six months ago, Leilani was assaulted by a man she had been seeing for several months following the death of her husband. The relationship had developed slowly and she had allowed herself, cautiously, to feel something again. On the evening of the assault, he had been drinking heavily - she had noticed the sharp, sweet-sour smell of alcohol on him the moment he arrived at her door - and what began as an embrace escalated rapidly into violence. He pinned her, and she found herself unable to move, unable to stop what was happening to her body. What stayed with her most viscerally afterward was not only the pain but a particular helplessness that felt total: her arms held, her voice gone, her strength useless. She had always considered herself capable, self-reliant, a woman who had raised children alone after her husband's illness and built a technical career in a field that rarely welcomed people who looked like her. That night dismantled something she had quietly relied upon.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani did not contact police. She had come to believe, in a way she could not fully articulate but felt with great certainty, that she had somehow permitted this - that she had opened a door she should have kept closed, and that in doing so she had acted against everything she believed herself to be. The shame she carried was not abstract. It lived in her body. She began avoiding mirrors. She stopped wearing the clothes she had liked. She ate very little, and then began controlling her meals with a precision that had nothing to do with nutrition - counting, restricting, scheduling - because it was the one domain in which she felt she could determine an outcome. She gave up the evening walks she had taken for years along the river path near her home, and she stopped attending her church community's monthly dinners, which had been a source of genuine pleasure since her husband's passing.

At work, Leilani sits in an open-plan office where colleagues occasionally pass behind her chair or place a hand briefly on her shoulder to get her attention. Each time this happens, her body responds before her mind can intervene - she startles violently, her chair scraping back, her breath gone. She has begun positioning herself with her back to the wall when possible and has developed a habit of scanning the room when she enters it, her eyes moving to the letter opener on a nearby desk, the heavy stapler, the glass partition she has calculated could shatter. She is aware that this is not rational, and the awareness itself distresses her. When colleagues have noticed her flinching and told her she is safe, that this is just the office, she has nodded and said nothing, because she has found it genuinely impossible to feel what they are describing. Safety, to Leilani, has become a word that belongs to other people.

She has not permitted anyone to hug her since the assault. When her adult daughter visited last Christmas and reached for her at the door, Leilani stepped back before she could stop herself. Her daughter looked hurt. Leilani said she had a cold. The distance between them has quietly widened since then, and Leilani knows it, and has not known how to close it - nor, she admits, has she been certain she wanted to.

What finally brought her to her physician was a moment at work when she sat in a server room alone and realised she could not remember the last time she had felt anything she would call pleasure. She is most afraid, she says, that this is simply who she is now. What she is hoping for, though she offers it tentatively, is some evidence that it isn't.
